extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and courts applying U.S. patent statutes (late 19th–early 20th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of U.S. federal patent statutes and related judiciary acts (1875–1902) setting substantive patentability rules, procedural requirements, fee schedules, remedies, venue/jurisdiction, and other regulatory standards relevant to patent practice and litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-term extension: grounds and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissioner may extend a patent for seven years from expiration of the first term if satisfied that the patentee, without neglect or fault, has failed to obtain from use and sale a reasonable remuneration for the time, ingenuity, and expense bestowed, and that extension is just and proper with due regard to the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: "if it shall appear to the satisfaction of the Commissioner that the patentee, without neglect or fault on his part, has failed to obtain ... a reasonable remuneration ... and that it is just and proper, having due regard to the public interest, that the term of the patent should be extended, the Commissioner shall make a certificate ... renewing and extending the patent for the term of seven years from the expiration of the first term." Certificate is recorded in the Patent Office and the patent shall have the same effect in law as though originally granted for twenty-one years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension benefits extend to assignees/grantees
rubrics_metrics.description: The benefit of a patent extension extends to assignees and grantees of the right to use the thing patented to the extent of their interest therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Section 4928): "The benefit of the extension of a patent shall extend to the assignees and grantees of the right to use the thing patented, to the extent of their interest therein."

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-patent eligibility (what may be patented)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who, by his own industry/genius/efforts/expense, has invented and produced any new and original design for a manufacture, bust, statue, alto-relievo, bas-relief, printing of fabrics, impression/ornament/print/picture to be placed on an article of manufacture, or any new useful original shape/configuration of an article of manufacture not known/used by others or patented/described in any printed publication before his invention, may obtain a patent upon payment of prescribed fee and due proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Section 4929) lists many categories (designs for manufacture, sculptures, fabric printing patterns, impressions/ornaments/prints/pictures, shape/configuration of articles) and the novelty requirement: "the same not having been known or used by others before his invention or production thereof, or patented or described in any printed publication." Proceedings are to be "the same as in cases of inventions or discoveries."

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner may dispense with design models
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner may dispense with models of designs when the design can be sufficiently represented by drawings or photographs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Section 4930): "The Commissioner may dispense with models of designs when the design can be sufficiently represented by drawings or photographs."

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-patent term options (applicant election)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents for designs may be granted for terms of three years and six months, or seven years, or fourteen years, as the applicant may elect in his application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Section 4931): "Patents for designs may be granted for the term of three years and six months, or for seven years, or for fourteen years, as the applicant may, in his application, elect."

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension entitlement for pre-1861 design patentees
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees of designs issued prior to March 2, 1861 shall be entitled to extension of their respective patents for the term of seven years in the same manner and under the same restrictions as provided for extension of patents for inventions or discoveries issued prior to that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Section 4932): grants 7‑year extensions for pre‑1861 design patents under same restrictions as invention patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: General application of invention-patent provisions to designs
rubrics_metrics.description: All regulations and provisions which apply to obtaining or protecting patents for inventions or discoveries, not inconsistent with this Title, shall apply to patents for designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Section 4933): "All the regulations and provisions which apply to obtaining or protecting patents for inventions or discoveries not inconsistent with the provisions of this Title, shall apply to patents for designs." (i.e., procedural and substantive cross-application except where inconsistent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-fees schedule (rates for filings, issues, appeals, copies, recordings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific fees are prescribed for a range of Patent Office services: filing original application (except design) $15; issuing original patent (except design) $20; design cases: 3.5 years $10, 7 years $15, 14 years $30; filing each caveat $10; re-issue application $30; filing each disclaimer $10; application for extension $50; granting each extension $50; first appeal from primary examiners to examiners-in-chief $10; appeal from examiners-in-chief to Commissioner $20; certified copies 10 cents per 100 words; recording assignments/agreements/powers: $1 up to 300 words, $2 for >300 up to 1000, $3 for >1000; copies of drawings at reasonable cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Section 4934) lists each rate. Use exact fee amounts as statutory requirements for payments to the Patent Office. "For copies of drawings, the reasonable cost of making them."

rubrics_metrics.name: Where and how patent fees may be paid; receipts; Treasury deposit
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-fees may be paid to the Commissioner of Patents, the Treasurer or assistant treasurers of the United States, designated depositaries, national banks, or receivers of public money designated by the Secretary of the Treasury; such officer shall give the depositor a receipt or certificate of deposit; all money received at the Patent-Office shall be paid into the Treasury as received without any deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Section 4935) explains authorized payees and that receipts/certificates shall be given; all monies go to Treasury without deduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treasurer authorized to refund mistaken payments upon Commissioner's certificate
rubrics_metrics.description: The Treasurer of the United States is authorized to pay back any sum mistakenly paid into the Treasury as for fees accruing at the Patent-Office upon a certificate being made to the Treasurer by the Commissioner of Patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Section 4936): permits Treasurer refunds when Commissioner certifies mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity trials in patent causes may empanel juries
rubrics_metrics.description: Circuit courts sitting in equity for trial of patent causes may empanel a jury of not less than five and not more than twelve persons, submit to them such questions of fact as the court deems expedient, and the verdict shall be treated and proceeded upon like issues sent from chancery to a court of law and returned with findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Patent Act of Feb 16, 1875, Section 2): describes jury size (5–12), submission of fact questions, and treatment of verdicts (same manner and effect as issues from chancery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-patent infringement prohibited; remedies and damages
rubrics_metrics.description: During the term of letters patent for a design, it is unlawful for any person other than the owner, without license, to apply the patented design or any colorable imitation to any article of manufacture for sale, or to sell/expose for sale such articles knowing the design has been applied; violator liable in amount of $250, and if total profit exceeds $250 liable for excess; owner may recover by action at law or bill in equity for an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Patent Act of 1887): makes application or sale of patented design/colorable imitation unlawful, sets minimum liability $250 and additional liability equal to excess profit, and provides remedies (law or equity) including injunction. Also provides that owner shall not recover twice for the same profit (prevents double recovery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit Courts of Appeals: patent appellate jurisdiction and certification to Supreme Court
rubrics_metrics.description: Circuit Courts of Appeals shall exercise appellate jurisdiction to review final decisions in District/Circuit Courts arising under the patent laws; their judgments/decrees shall be final in all patent cases subject to the Circuit Court's ability to certify questions of law to the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court may instruct or require the whole record be sent up for full consideration; Supreme Court may also require certification of any such case for its review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Judiciary Act of 1891, Section 6 & related): establishes appellate review structure, finality of Circuit Courts of Appeals in patent matters, procedures for certification and Supreme Court instruction or review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory appeals of injunctions/receiverships in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where on a hearing in equity an injunction is granted/continued or a receiver appointed by interlocutory order/decree in a case with an appealable final decree, an appeal may be taken from such interlocutory order to the Circuit Court of Appeals provided the appeal is taken within thirty days from entry; such appeals take precedence in the appellate court; the proceedings below are not stayed unless ordered, and the court below may require an additional bond as condition of the appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Judiciary Act of 1891, Section 7): 30‑day time limit for interlocutory appeals relating to injunctions/receivers, precedence, stay rule, and possible bond condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit for appeals/writs of error to Circuit Courts of Appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: No appeal or writ of error to the Circuit Courts of Appeals shall be taken or sued out except within six months after the entry of the order, judgment, or decree sought to be reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Judiciary Act of 1891, Section 11): establishes a six‑month limitations window for appeals/writs seeking review in the Circuit Courts of Appeals; other existing rules regulating appeals/writs of error apply (methods, bonds, securities, allowances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court of Appeals for D.C.: review where patent validity involved regardless of amount
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court of Appeals of the District of Columbia may review final orders/judgments from the Supreme Court of the District of Columbia; determinations of appeals from the Commissioner of Patents and appeals in interference cases are vested in that Court; the Supreme Court may re-examine Court of Appeals' judgments where the matter in dispute exceeds five thousand dollars or where the validity of any patent or statute is involved irrespective of amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Judiciary Act of 1893, Sections 7–9): creates D.C. Court of Appeals, vests appeals from Commissioner of Patents, and permits Supreme Court review in patent-validity questions regardless of monetary amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue/jurisdiction for patent-infringement suits (1897)
rubrics_metrics.description: In suits brought for infringement of letters patent, the Circuit Courts shall have jurisdiction in the district of which the defendant is an inhabitant, or in any district in which the defendant has committed acts of infringement and has a regular and established place of business; if suit is brought where defendant is not an inhabitant but has such a place of business, service may be made upon the agent(s) engaged in conducting such business in that district.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Jurisdiction Act of 1897): specifies proper districts for bringing infringement suits and authorizes service on local agents when defendant's business exists in district.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / prior-publication / on-sale / public-use bars (amended Section 4886)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable, an invention must be new and useful, not known or used by others in this country before his invention, and not patented or described in any printed publication before his invention or more than two years prior to his application; also not in public use or on sale in this country for more than two years prior to application unless shown to have been abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (amendment to Section 4886 in Patent Act of 1897): "Any person who has invented or discovered any new and useful art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter ... not known or used by others in this country, before his invention ... and not patented or described in any printed publication ... before his invention ... or more than two years prior to his application, and not in public use or on sale in this country for more than two years prior to his application, unless the same is proved to have been abandoned, may ... obtain a patent therefor." (establishes novelty and two‑year statutory bars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses in infringement actions (special matters defendant may prove)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an action for infringement the defendant, after 30 days' written notice to plaintiff/attorney, may prove one or more special matters: (1) the specification was made to contain less than the whole truth or more than necessary to produce the effect (fraud/deception); (2) the patentee surreptitiously or unjustly obtained the patent which was in fact invented by another who used reasonable diligence; (3) it had been patented or described in some printed publication prior to supposed invention or more than two years prior to application; (4) the patentee was not the original and first inventor of any material and substantial part; (5) it had been in public use or on sale in the country for more than two years before application or had been abandoned to the public. If any special matter is found for defendant, judgment shall be rendered for him with costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (amendment to Section 4920 in Patent Act of 1897) lists the five defenses explicitly and requires defendant to state names/dates/places in notices re previous invention/knowledge/use. The same defenses apply in equity suits with like notice and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patent filing more than seven months before U.S. filing bars U.S. patent
rubrics_metrics.description: No person otherwise entitled shall be debarred from receiving a patent because it was first patented in a foreign country by the inventor or his representatives, unless the application for that foreign patent was filed more than seven months prior to the filing of the application in this country, in which case no patent shall be granted in this country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (amendment to Section 4887 in Patent Act of 1897) inserts the seven‑month foreign filing bar rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications must be completed/prepared for examination within one year or be abandoned
rubrics_metrics.description: All applications for patents shall be completed and prepared for examination within one year after filing, and failure to do so, or failure to prosecute within one year after any action (after notice), shall be regarded as abandonment unless shown to the satisfaction of the Commissioner that the delay was unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (amendment to Section 4894 in Patent Act of 1897): changed prior two‑year defaults to one year and sets default/abandonment rule subject to Commissioner's discretion for unavoidable delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments: form, recording, and prima facie evidence of acknowledgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent or any interest therein shall be assignable by instrument in writing; such assignment/grant/conveyance is void against subsequent purchaser or mortgagee for valuable consideration without notice unless recorded in the Patent Office within three months from its date. If acknowledged before specified officers (notary public, commissioner of U.S. circuit court, secretary of legation or consular officer authorized), the certificate of acknowledgment under hand and official seal shall be prima facie evidence of execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (amendment to Section 4898 in Patent Act of 1897): describes recordation time window (three months), and lists officers whose acknowledgment certificates are prima facie evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on recovery of profits/damages (six-year lookback)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any suit or action for the infringement of any patent there shall be no recovery of profits or damages for any infringement committed more than six years before the filing of the bill of complaint or the issuing of the writ in such suit or action; this provision applies to existing causes of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (amendment to Section 4921 in Patent Act of 1897): imposes a six‑year statute-of-limitation cap on recoverable past damages/profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department-head requests to expedite must be represented before Commissioner
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the head of any Department of the Government requests the Commissioner of Patents to expedite consideration of an application, it is the duty of such head to be represented before the Commissioner to prevent the improper issue of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Section 7 of Patent Act of 1897) places duty on Department heads to be represented when seeking expedited action to avoid improper issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to apply on death or insanity devolves to legal representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: When a person who has made a new invention dies before a patent is granted, the right of applying for and obtaining the patent shall devolve on his executor or administrator in trust for heirs or devisees as appropriate; if the inventor becomes insane before a patent is granted, the right devolves on his legally appointed guardian, conservator, or representative in trust for his estate, with the oath/affirmation to be varied for such representatives. (Applies to existing and future applications as to insane persons.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (Patent Act of 1899, amendment to Section 4896) extends application rights to executors/administrators/guardians and permits variation of required oath/affirmation when applied by legal representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and signing of letters patent (issuance formalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: All patents shall be issued in the name of the United States of America, under the seal of the Patent Office, and shall be signed by the Commissioner of Patents, and they shall be recorded, together with the specifications, in the Patent Office in books to be kept for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording (amendment to Section 4883 in Patent Act of April 1902): specifies issuance formalities and requires Commissioner signature and recording with specifications.
